title: A Letter for the Autopsy
premise: Retired detective Astrid Hartwell receives a confession letter for a drowning case she worked decades ago — postmarked the day after the victim's funeral, naming details never made public. As she reopens the file from her failing bookshop, she realizes the writer knows the investigation better than any investigator, feeding her clues that lead toward the coastal town where the body was found. The killer is someone who lived inside the case all along: the victim's grieving sister, who staged her own death to finally be seen. Astrid traps her at the tideline with the truth — and chooses to close the bookshop's back room as a home for the found family they've both been missing.
about_author: Mara Crane is a former small-town newspaper reporter who spent ten years covering cold cases along the northern coast before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about memory, tide, and the families we build when the ones we're given fail us.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Sorting dead-stock in her failing bookshop, Astrid opens a confession letter for the 1987 drowning of Elin Voss — postmarked the day after Elin's funeral, though Elin died thirty years ago. The letter names a detail only the lead detective knew: her. Emotional beat: dread wrapped in flattery; the hook of being personally addressed by a ghost.

chapters.title: The File That Breathes
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She retrieves her private copy of the Voss case file and finds pages annotated in fresh ink — corrections to her own old conclusions, each one accurate. A second letter arrives inviting her to 'finish what you started.' Emotional beat: professional humiliation curdling into obsession; the case knows her better than she remembers it.

chapters.title: Salt on the Margins
chapters.summary: Alternating POV introduces Juniper Voss, Elin's younger sister, tending the family house above the tideline, receiving gentle anonymous letters of condolence. Astrid travels to the coastal town and interviews the original coroner, now dying, who insists the body was moved after death. Emotional beat: unease — two people are being written to by the same invisible hand.

chapters.title: What the Tide Took Twice
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Reconstructing the scene, Astrid finds the original search grid was drawn wrong — deliberately, she suspects, by someone on the force. The third letter arrives with a photograph of her own bookshop, taken from across the street. Emotional beat: violation; the game has followed her home, and the hunter realizes she is also bait.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Waited
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper recalls the night Elin died — the argument, the storm, the lie she told at seventeen that closed the case too neatly. She begins answering the anonymous letters, confessing her guilt to a stranger who may not exist. Emotional beat: grief as a locked room; Juniper wants absolution more than safety.

chapters.title: A Detail Too Far
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Cross-referencing letters against the file, Astrid notices the writer quotes a sentence from her unpublished personal notebook — meaning the confessor had access to her home or her past self. She sets a trap: a false detail planted in a public records request. Emotional beat: cold clarity; the detective stops chasing and starts building a cage.

chapters.title: The Funeral That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper attends the memorial for 'Elin' and watches the coffin lowered — empty, she is suddenly certain, because she buried her sister's secrets long ago and knows how this town buries things. The anonymous letters turn darker, urging her to 'come to the water.' Emotional beat: vertigo; Juniper realizes she has been groomed toward a shoreline.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Her trap springs: the false detail surfaces verbatim in a new letter, narrowing suspects to those with access to both the file and her life — and pointing, impossibly, toward the Voss house. Racing the spring tide, Astrid drives through the storm to intercept whoever Juniper is about to meet. Emotional beat: accelerating panic; every clue converges on one address and one hour.

chapters.title: The Confession at the Tideline
chapters.summary: Dual POV climax. At the water's edge, Astrid finds Juniper — and learns Juniper wrote the letters herself, splitting into 'the confessor' to force the truth out of the town that let Elin die, staging the funeral as the final lure. Astrid disarms the moment not with handcuffs but with the one thing Juniper never had: someone who believes her. Emotional beat: catharsis; the trap closes around grief, not a monster.

chapters.title: Shelf Life
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, weeks later. The true circumstances of Elin's death are quietly reopened; Juniper, awaiting trial, asks Astrid to keep writing to her. Astrid converts the bookshop's back room into a reading room for the town's lost kids — a found family in brick and paper. Final letter arrives: 'Case closed?' She writes back: 'Closed. Not forgotten.' Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; identity rebuilt from what remains.
